paragraphs: Eurypylus, the brave son of Euaemon, saw that the rain of arrows was overpowering Ajax. He went up to him and hurled his spear, and it struck Apisaon son of Phausius in the liver, below the midriff, and laid him low. Eurypylus sprang on him and stripped the armor from his shoulders. But Paris saw him at it and aimed an arrow at him. It hit him in the right thigh and broke off, and the point left in the wound dragged at the thigh. So Eurypylus drew back among his comrades to save his life. As he went, he shouted to the Danaans, “My friends, princes and counselors of the Argives, rally to the defense of Ajax, who is being overpowered. I doubt he will come out of this fight alive. Come here, then, and rescue great Ajax son of Telamon.”

He cried out like this when he was wounded, and the others came near and gathered around him, holding their shields up from their shoulders to cover him. Ajax then moved toward them, and as soon as he reached his men he turned around to stand at bay.

So they fought, like a flaming fire. Meanwhile the mares of Neleus, all in a lather of sweat, were carrying Nestor out of the fight, and Machaon, shepherd of his people, with him. Achilles saw them and took note. He was standing on the stern of his ship, watching the hard stress and struggle of the battle. He called out from the ship to his comrade Patroclus. Patroclus heard him in the tent and came out looking like Ares himself—this was the beginning of the evil that soon befell him. “Achilles,” he said, “why do you call me? What do you want with me?” Achilles answered, “Noble son of Menoetius, man after my own heart, I think the Achaeans will soon be praying at my knees, for they are in great straits. Go, Patroclus, and ask Nestor who it is that he is carrying away wounded from the field. From behind I would say it was Machaon son of Asclepius, but I could not see his face, because the horses went past me at full speed.”
Patroclus did what his dear comrade had told him and ran off past the ships and tents of the Achaeans.

Nestor and Machaon reached the tents of the son of Neleus and dismounted, and an esquire, Eurymedon, took the horses from the chariot. The two men stood in the breeze by the seaside to dry the sweat from their shirts. Then they went inside and took their seats. Fair Hecamede mixed them a mess. Nestor had been awarded her from Tenedos when Achilles took it; she was the daughter of wise Arsinous, and the Achaeans had given her to Nestor because he excelled all of them in counsel. First she set before them a fair, well-made table with feet of cyanus. On it were a bronze vessel, an onion to give relish to the drink, and honey and cakes of barley meal. There was also a cup of rare workmanship that the old man had brought from home, studded with bosses of gold. It had four handles, and on each handle two golden doves were feeding; it stood on two feet. Anyone else would hardly have been able to lift it from the table when it was full, but Nestor lifted it quite easily. In this cup the woman, as fair as a goddess, mixed them a mess with Pramnian wine. She grated goat’s milk cheese into it with a bronze grater and threw in a handful of white barley meal. When the mess was ready she told them to drink it. They drank and quenched their thirst, and then they fell to talking with one another. At this moment Patroclus appeared at the door.

The old man saw him, sprang from his seat, seized his hand and led him into the tent, and told him to take a place among them. But Patroclus stayed where he was. “Noble sir,” he said, “I may not stay. You cannot persuade me to come in. The man who sent me is not one to be trifled with, and he told me to ask who the wounded man was that you were carrying away from the field. I can see for myself now that it is Machaon, shepherd of his people. I must go back and tell Achilles. You, sir, know what a terrible man he is, and how ready to blame even where no blame is due.”

Nestor answered, “Why should Achilles care to know how many of the Achaeans are wounded? He pays no heed to the dismay that reigns in our host. Our most valiant chieftains lie disabled. Brave Diomedes, son of Tydeus, is wounded, and so are Odysseus and Agamemnon. Eurypylus has been hit in the thigh with an arrow, and I have just brought this man from the field, also wounded with an arrow. Yet Achilles, valiant as he is, does not care and knows no pity. Will he wait until the ships are in a blaze, do what we may, and we perish one on top of another? As for me, I have no strength or staying power left. I wish I were still young and strong, as in the days when a fight broke out between us and the men of Elis over some cattle raiding. I killed Itymoneus then, the valiant son of Hypeirochus, who lived in Elis. I was driving off the spoil, and he was hit by a dart thrown from my hand as he fought in the front rank to defend his cows. He fell, and the country people around him were in great fear. We drove off a vast quantity of booty from the plain: fifty herds of cattle and as many flocks of sheep, fifty droves of pigs, and as many wide-spreading flocks of goats. We also seized a hundred and fifty horses, all of them mares, and many had foals running with them. We drove all these by night to Pylus, the city of Neleus, and took them inside the city. Neleus was glad that I had taken so much, though it was the first time I had ever been in the field. At daybreak the heralds went around crying that all in Elis who were owed a debt should come, and the leading Pylians assembled to divide the spoils. The Epeans owed chattels to many people, for we men of Pylus were few and had been oppressed with wrong. In former years Heracles had come and laid his hand heavy on us, and all our best men had perished. Neleus had had twelve sons, but I alone was left; the others had all been killed. The Epeans presumed on all this, looked down on us and did us much evil. My father chose a herd of cattle and a great flock of sheep, three hundred in all, and took their shepherds with him. A great debt was due to him in Elis, namely four prize-winning horses. They and their chariots had gone to the games to run for a tripod, but King Augeas took them and sent back their driver, grieving for the loss of his horses. Neleus was angered by what Augeas had said and done, and took great value in return. The rest he divided, so that no man would have less than his full share.

“So we arranged everything and offered sacrifices to the gods throughout the city. Three days later the Epeans came in a body, many in number, with their chariots, in full array. The two Moliones came with them in their armor, though they were still lads and unused to fighting. Now there is a certain town, Thryoessa, perched on a rock by the river Alpheus, the border city of Pylus. The Epeans wanted to destroy it, and they pitched their camp around it. But when they had crossed their whole plain, Athena darted down by night from Olympus and told us to set ourselves in array. She found willing soldiers in Pylos, for the men meant to fight. Neleus would not let me arm. He hid my horses, for he said I could not yet know anything about war. Nevertheless Athena so ordered the fight that I, all on foot as I was, fought among our mounted forces and vied with the foremost of them. There is a river Minyeius that falls into the sea near Arene. There those of us who were mounted (and I with them) waited until morning, when the companies of foot soldiers came up with us in force. From there, in full panoply and equipment, we came toward noon to the sacred waters of the Alpheus. There we offered victims to almighty Zeus, with a bull to Alpheus, another to Poseidon, and a herd heifer to Athena. After this we took supper in our companies and lay down to rest, each in his armor, by the river.

“The Epeans were besieging the city and were determined to take it, but before that could happen a desperate fight was in store for them. When the sun’s rays began to fall on the earth we joined battle, praying to Zeus and Athena. Once the fight had begun, I was the first to kill my man and take his horses, the warrior Mulius. He was son-in-law to Augeas, married to his eldest daughter, golden-haired Agamede, who knew the virtues of every herb that grows on the face of the earth. I speared him as he came toward me. When he fell headlong in the dust I sprang onto his chariot and took my place in the front ranks. The Epeans fled in all directions when they saw the captain of their horsemen, the best man they had, laid low. I swept down on them like a whirlwind and took fifty chariots, and in each of them two men bit the dust, slain by my spear. I would even have killed the two Moliones, sons of Actor, if their real father, Poseidon, lord of the earthquake, had not hidden them in a thick mist and carried them out of the fight. Then Zeus granted the Pylians a great victory. We chased the Epeans far over the plain, killing the men and gathering their armor, until we brought our horses to Buprasium, rich in wheat, and to the Olenian rock, and the hill called Alision, where Athena turned the people back. There I killed the last man and left him. Then the Achaeans drove their horses back from Buprasium to Pylos, and gave thanks to Zeus among the gods, and among mortal men to Nestor.

“That is what I was among my peers, as surely as ever any man was, but Achilles means to keep all his valor for himself. He will bitterly regret it later, when the host is being cut to pieces. My good friend, did Menoetius not give you this charge on the day he sent you from Phthia to Agamemnon? Odysseus and I were inside the house and heard everything he said to you. We had come to the fair house of Peleus while recruiting throughout all Achaea, and when we arrived we found Menoetius and yourself there, and Achilles with you. The old knight Peleus was in the outer court, roasting the fat thigh-bones of a heifer for Zeus, lord of thunder. He held a gold chalice in his hand and poured drink offerings of wine over the burning sacrifice. You two were busy cutting up the heifer, and just then we stood at the gates. Achilles sprang to his feet, led us by the hand into the house, seated us at table, and set before us the hospitality that guests expect. When we had had enough meat and drink, I said my say and urged both of you to join us. You were ready enough, and the two old men gave you many strict charges. Old Peleus told his son Achilles to fight always among the foremost and to outdo his peers. Menoetius the son of Actor spoke to you like this: ‘My son, Achilles is of nobler birth than you, but you are older than he, though he is far the better man of the two. Counsel him wisely, guide him the right way, and he will follow you to his own profit.’ That was your father’s charge to you, but you have forgotten it. Even now, though, say all this to Achilles, if he will listen to you. Who knows whether, with heaven’s help, you may talk him over? It is good to take a friend’s advice. But if he is fearful about some oracle, or if his mother has told him something from Zeus, then let him send you, and let the rest of the Myrmidons follow with you, in case you may bring light and rescue to the Danaans. And let him send you into battle dressed in his own armor, so that the Trojans may mistake you for him and stop fighting. The sons of the Achaeans may then have time to get their breath, for they are hard pressed and there is little breathing time in battle. You are fresh, and might easily drive a tired enemy back to his walls, away from the tents and ships.”

Nestor’s words moved the heart of Patroclus, and he ran off along the line of the ships toward Achilles, descendant of Aeacus. Near the ships of Odysseus, where the Achaeans held their assemblies and their court of justice, and where their altars to the gods stood, he met Eurypylus son of Euaemon. Eurypylus was limping out of the fight with an arrow in his thigh. Sweat rained from his head and shoulders, and black blood welled from his cruel wound, yet his mind did not wander. The son of Menoetius felt compassion at the sight and spoke to him piteously. “Unhappy princes and counselors of the Danaans! Are you doomed, then, to feed the hounds of Troy with your fat, far from your friends and your native land? Tell me, noble Eurypylus, can the Achaeans hold great Hector in check, or will they fall now before his spear?”

Wounded Eurypylus answered, “Noble Patroclus, the Achaeans have no hope left. They will perish at their ships. Every man who was a prince among us lies struck down and wounded by the Trojans, and the Trojans are growing stronger and stronger. But save me. Take me to your ship, cut the arrow out of my thigh, and wash the black blood from it with warm water. Then lay on it those gracious herbs that Achilles showed you, so they say, and that Chiron, most righteous of all the centaurs, showed to him. As for the physicians Podalirius and Machaon, I hear that one is lying wounded in his tent and needs healing himself, while the other is fighting the Trojans on the plain.”

“Hero Eurypylus,” the brave son of Menoetius replied, “what can be done? How can this be? I am on my way to noble Achilles with a message from Nestor of Gerene, bulwark of the Achaeans. Even so, I will not forget your distress.”

With this he put his arm around Eurypylus’s middle and led him into the tent. A servant saw him and spread bullock-skins on the ground for him to lie on. Patroclus laid him at full length and cut the sharp arrow out of his thigh. He washed the black blood from the wound with warm water. Then he crushed a bitter herb between his hands and spread it on the wound. This was a virtuous herb that killed all pain, and the wound soon dried and the blood stopped flowing.
